name: Inveigh (PowerShell) - LLMNR/NBNS Poisoning
description: Windows PowerShell LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoner — the Responder equivalent for when you already have a Windows foothold and no Linux box on-segment. Captures NTLMv2 hashes from other hosts on the same subnet. Note: the PS version is deprecated in favor of the C# Inveigh.exe.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHY INVEIGH EXISTS ===
LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning requires L2 access (same subnet as victims). If you land
on a Windows host via phishing, RCE, or credential reuse, you can't run Linux
Responder. Inveigh is the Windows-native equivalent — pure PowerShell (or C#),
no additional binaries needed beyond the script.

=== POWERSHELL VERSION (this card) vs C# VERSION ===
  Invoke-Inveigh (PS)  → older, deprecated, but runs anywhere PS is available
  Inveigh.exe (C#)     → active development, interactive console, preferred choice
  Use PS version when: .exe execution is blocked but PS isn't, or you're on an
  old system without the .exe available.

=== IMPORT AND RUN ===
  Import-Module .\Inveigh.ps1
  Invoke-Inveigh Y -NBNS Y -ConsoleOutput Y -FileOutput Y

Flags:
  Y (first)         → enable LLMNR poisoning
  -NBNS Y           → also poison NBT-NS (broader coverage)
  -ConsoleOutput Y  → print captures to console in real time
  -FileOutput Y     → save to Inveigh-NTLMv2.txt in current dir

=== WHAT TO LOOK FOR ===
  NTLMV2 captured for [user] from [IP]
Look for: domain user accounts, service accounts (svc-*, sql-*, backup-*)
Machine accounts (HOSTNAME$) are low value — rarely crack.

=== OUTPUT FILES ===
  Inveigh-Log.txt      → event log
  Inveigh-NTLMv2.txt  → captured hashes (ready for Hashcat -m 5600)

=== OPSEC ===
Loud — LLMNR responses from a non-DC are suspicious. Security tools (MDI,
Defender for Identity) flag this behavior. Run during business hours briefly
to blend with legitimate authentication noise rather than all day.

defense.why_it_works: Inveigh (PowerShell) is a Windows LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS spoofer that captures NetNTLM hashes from a Windows foothold (no Linux attacker box needed).
defense.prerequisites: A PowerShell foothold on a host in the victim segment.
defense.impact: NetNTLM hashes captured from within Windows for cracking/relay.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1557.001] LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS responses from an unexpected host; a spoofed name-resolution answer; NetNTLM auth to an unknown host. Honeypot name-lookups (queries for non-existent hosts) that get answered reveal poisoning; Defender for Identity flags it. Inveigh runs as a PowerShell script (4104 script-block logging).
defense.artifacts: Spoofed answers; captured hashes; Inveigh in 4104 logs.
defense.prevention: Disable LLMNR, NBT-NS, and mDNS (GPO/registry); require SMB signing to block relay; segment; deploy honeytoken name-lookups to catch poisoners; enforce authenticated DNS.
defense.evasion: In-memory execution and selective spoofing reduce artifacts; obfuscation dodges AMSI/script signatures.
defense.misconfiguration: LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution, UDP 5355) and NBT-NS (NetBIOS Name Service, UDP 137) are enabled by default on Windows and are used as fallback name resolution when DNS fails. These protocols broadcast name queries on the local network segment. Any host on the same subnet can respond to these broadcasts — a Responder instance claims to be the queried host and captures the NTLMv2 hash when the victim tries to authenticate.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# LLMNR enabled (Windows default):
# Registry: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient
#   EnableMulticast: (not set or 1) = LLMNR active

# NBT-NS enabled (Windows default):
# Network adapter -> TCP/IP properties -> WINS -> 'Enable NetBIOS over TCP/IP'
# = Default (or Enabled)

# Test: trigger a failed DNS lookup, watch Responder capture NTLMv2:
# net use \\nonexistent  -> host broadcasts LLMNR for 'nonexistent'
# Responder replies -> host sends NTLMv2 -> Responder captures it
defense.secure_config:
# Disable LLMNR via GPO:
# Computer Config > Admin Templates > Network > DNS Client
#   'Turn off multicast name resolution' = Enabled
# OR Registry:
Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient' \
    -Name EnableMulticast -Value 0

# Disable NBT-NS via GPO (push WMI script or DHCP option 001 = 0x2):
# Or per-machine:
Get-WmiObject Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration | ForEach-Object {
    $_.SetTcpipNetbios(2)  # 2 = Disable NetBIOS
}

# Enable SMB signing (stops relay attacks even if hash captured):
Set-SmbServerConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $true -Force
